name: Ear shaping / elfing

lead: Ear shaping, or elfing, changes the upper ear into a pointed outline similar to fantasy elves. Pointed ears are a long-standing fictional trait seen in elves, Vulcans and other characters, and from the 2020s some people have worn latex ears or had their ears surgically reshaped.

Most patients are reported to be women who believe the pointed ears make their faces look smaller, and the procedure has been described as a sought-after enhancement in parts of Asia. It is relatively new, and its long-term effects are not established.

paras: Non-surgical routes include prosthetic latex ear tips worn over the ears. Surgical routes involve a cosmetic surgeon reshaping the ear cartilage and skin; details of technique are a matter for a qualified surgeon and are not described here.

Reports describe it as experimental, with unknown long-term effects, and a 2026 case linked to complications was reported with a headline describing facial paralysis. Mainstream health bodies in many places have not accredited it.

angle.text: People choose it to change the ear's silhouette, and patients report that it makes the face appear smaller. The effect is a stated perception rather than a measured outcome.

lead: Ear shaping, often called elfing, refers to changing ear shape to a pointed form. Pointed ears are shorthand for 'not human' in fiction, from elves and goblins to Star Trek's Vulcans, and Tolkien film adaptations are credited with popularising the look [1].

In the 2020s people have worn latex elf ears and, in some cases, had ears surgically reshaped. In 2026 the Wall Street Journal called elf ears the most coveted enhancement in Asia, especially China and Korea [1]. Most patients are described as women who think pointed ears make their faces look smaller [1].

Sources describe the procedure as relatively new and experimental, with unknown long-term effects and no accreditation from mainstream health bodies in many places, and mention a 2026 case with reported complications including facial paralysis [1].

paras: Pointed ears appear in older folklore such as satyrs and leprechauns, and Victorian literature tied them to elves [1]. The popular association strengthened through film and games, which provided the visual vocabulary for the later body-modification trend [1].
Patients cited in reports say the shape makes the face look smaller, and the trend has been reported as especially popular in China and Korea in the mid-2020s [1].

The reported risks include complications from a 2026 case where a headline described facial paralysis, and uncertainty about long-term effects because the procedure is new and not accredited by mainstream health bodies in many places [1].
No studies found on elf ear procedures. Related registered trials concern ear reconstruction for microtia, a different indication, such as the Auryzon system [2] and a bioprinted-implant study [3].
